notes:
1. Vijayanagara Empire — Overview

  • The Vijayanagara Empire emerged in South India in the fourteenth century.
  • It was founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka I.
  • Its capital was Vijayanagara, whose ruins are at present-day Hampi in Karnataka.
  • The empire became one of the most powerful states of medieval South India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara Empire → 1336 → Harihara I + Bukka I

2. Meaning of Vijayanagara

  • Vijayanagara means "City of Victory."
  • The imperial capital developed on the banks of the Tungabhadra River.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vijayanagara / Hampi → Tungabhadra River

3. Hampi

  • Hampi is located in present-day Karnataka.
  • It contains the ruins of the Vijayanagara imperial capital.
  • Its landscape combines:
  • Granite hills.
  • Tungabhadra River.
  • Fortifications.
  • Temples.
  • Palaces.
  • Markets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara Capital → Hampi

4. Founders

  • Harihara I and Bukka I were brothers.
  • They belonged to the Sangama family.
  • They established the first ruling dynasty of Vijayanagara.

5. Sangama Dynasty

  • The Sangama dynasty was the first dynasty of Vijayanagara.
  • It ruled from the foundation of the empire in 1336 until the late fifteenth century.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Vijayanagara Dynasty → Sangama

6. Vidyaranya

  • Vijayanagara tradition strongly associates the sage-scholar Vidyaranya with Harihara and Bukka.
  • He was linked with the Sringeri Sharada Peetham.
  • Later accounts credit him with providing ideological and spiritual support to the founders.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Vidyaranya → Traditionally Associated with Foundation; Exact Political Role Is Debated

7. Four Dynasties of Vijayanagara

The empire was ruled by four dynasties:

  • Sangama.
  • Saluva.
  • Tuluva.
  • Aravidu.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu

8. Vijayanagara and Delhi Sultanate Context

  • Vijayanagara emerged during a period of political instability in the Deccan and South India.
  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq's attempts to control the Deccan weakened.
  • Independent regional powers emerged.

9. Vijayanagara and Bahmani Sultanate

  • Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate emerged as major rival powers in the Deccan.
  • Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347.
  • Their rivalry continued for generations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara → 1336

Bahmani → 1347

10. Raichur Doab

  • One of the most contested regions between Vijayanagara and Deccan powers was the Raichur Doab.
  • It lies between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raichur Doab → Between Krishna and Tungabhadra

11. Why Raichur Doab Was Important

The region was valuable because of:

  • Fertile agricultural land.
  • Strategic forts.
  • Revenue.
  • Control of routes across the Deccan.

12. Harihara I

  • Harihara I was one of the founders of Vijayanagara.
  • He consolidated authority in the Tungabhadra region.
  • He laid the foundation of the Sangama state.

13. Bukka I

  • Bukka I succeeded Harihara I.
  • Under him the empire expanded substantially.
  • Vijayanagara influence extended into southern and eastern regions.

14. Kumara Kampana

  • Kumara Kampana was the son of Bukka I.
  • He led the famous Vijayanagara campaign into the Tamil region.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kumara Kampana → Vijayanagara Conquest of Madurai

15. Madurai Sultanate

  • The Madurai Sultanate had emerged in the fourteenth century following the weakening of Delhi Sultanate authority in South India.
  • It controlled parts of the Tamil region.

16. Vijayanagara Campaign Against Madurai

  • Kumara Kampana defeated the Madurai Sultanate during the later fourteenth century.
  • Vijayanagara authority then expanded deeply into Tamil country.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vijayanagara Expansion into Tamil Nadu → Kumara Kampana

17. Madura Vijayam

  • Madura Vijayam is an important Sanskrit work describing Kumara Kampana's southern campaign.
  • It was written by Gangadevi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Madura Vijayam → Gangadevi → Kumara Kampana

18. Gangadevi

  • Gangadevi was the wife of Kumara Kampana.
  • Her Madura Vijayam is an important literary source for Vijayanagara expansion into the Tamil region.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Gangadevi → Madura Vijayam

19. Importance of Madurai Conquest

The conquest:

  • Ended the Madurai Sultanate's dominance.
  • Extended Vijayanagara influence into Tamil Nadu.
  • Strengthened protection and patronage of major temples.
  • Laid groundwork for later Vijayanagara-Nayak administration.

20. Srirangam

  • Srirangam became an important religious centre under Vijayanagara patronage.
  • Restoration and renewed temple patronage followed periods of political disruption.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Vijayanagara → Srirangam Temple Patronage

21. Vijayanagara and Tamil Temple Centres

Important Tamil religious centres receiving Vijayanagara or later Nayak patronage included:

  • Srirangam.
  • Kanchipuram.
  • Tiruvannamalai.
  • Chidambaram.
  • Madurai.
  • Rameswaram.

22. Harihara II

  • Harihara II expanded Vijayanagara influence during the late fourteenth century.
  • The empire strengthened control over:
  • Karnataka.
  • Andhra regions.
  • Parts of the western coast.

23. Western Coastal Trade

  • Control over western coastal routes was important for:
  • Horse imports.
  • Maritime commerce.
  • Customs revenue.
  • Contact with Arabian traders.

24. Devaraya I

  • Devaraya I was an important Sangama ruler.
  • His reign saw continuing conflict over the Raichur Doab.

25. Irrigation Under Devaraya I

  • Devaraya I is associated with major irrigation works around Vijayanagara.
  • Dams and channels helped bring Tungabhadra water toward the capital.
📌 Must-Memorise

Devaraya I → Irrigation Works

26. Tungabhadra Irrigation

  • Vijayanagara's dry environment made water management essential.
  • Reservoirs, tanks and canals supported:
  • Agriculture.
  • Urban population.
  • Royal gardens.

27. Devaraya II

  • Devaraya II was one of the greatest rulers of the Sangama dynasty.
  • He ruled during the first half of the fifteenth century.
📌 Must-Memorise

Great Sangama Ruler → Devaraya II

28. Devaraya II's Titles

  • Literary traditions praise Devaraya II as a powerful and cultured king.
  • He is sometimes associated with the title Gajabetekara, meaning elephant hunter.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gajabetekara → Devaraya II

29. Devaraya II and Military Reform

  • Devaraya II strengthened his military organisation.
  • Contemporary accounts indicate greater recruitment of skilled Muslim cavalrymen and archers.

30. Cavalry Problem

  • South Indian kingdoms had difficulty breeding sufficient high-quality war horses.
  • Horses were therefore imported from:
  • Arabia.
  • Persia.
  • Persian Gulf regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara Military Weakness → Dependence on Imported Horses

31. Horse Trade

  • Control of horse imports was strategically crucial.
  • West-coast ports became extremely important to Vijayanagara rulers.

32. Abdur Razzaq

  • Persian traveller Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara in 1443 during Devaraya II's reign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Abdur Razzaq → Devaraya II → 1443

33. Abdur Razzaq's Account

  • He described Vijayanagara as:
  • Large.
  • Wealthy.
  • Strongly fortified.
  • Commercially active.
  • His account is one of the most important foreign descriptions of the capital.

34. Vijayanagara Fortifications

  • The capital had multiple defensive enclosures.
  • Natural granite hills were integrated into the fortification system.

35. Decline of Sangama Dynasty

  • After Devaraya II, weak rulers and internal struggles weakened central authority.
  • Powerful military commanders gained influence.

36. Saluva Narasimha

  • Saluva Narasimha seized power in the late fifteenth century.
  • He established the Saluva dynasty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Founder of Saluva Dynasty → Saluva Narasimha

37. Saluva Dynasty

  • The Saluva dynasty was short-lived.
  • Its rise represented an attempt to prevent political disintegration.

38. Narasa Nayaka

  • Tuluva Narasa Nayaka became the dominant military leader after Saluva Narasimha.
  • He served as regent and effectively controlled the empire.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narasa Nayaka → Foundation for Tuluva Power

39. Tuluva Dynasty

  • The Tuluva dynasty succeeded the Saluvas.
  • It produced the most famous Vijayanagara emperor:
  • Krishnadevaraya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Krishnadevaraya → Tuluva Dynasty

40. Vira Narasimha

  • Vira Narasimha was an early Tuluva ruler.
  • He was succeeded by Krishnadevaraya.

41. Krishnadevaraya

  • Krishnadevaraya became emperor in 1509.
  • He ruled until 1529.
  • His reign is traditionally regarded as the political and cultural high point of Vijayanagara.
📌 Must-Memorise

Krishnadevaraya → 1509–1529

42. Krishnadevaraya's Political Position

He faced important rivals including:

  • Deccan Sultanates.
  • Gajapati rulers of Odisha.
  • Rebellious provincial chiefs.

43. Krishnadevaraya and the Deccan

  • He fought successfully against the Deccan Sultanates.
  • The Raichur Doab remained a major area of conflict.

44. Raichur Campaign

  • Krishnadevaraya captured Raichur after defeating Bijapur forces in 1520.
📌 Must-Memorise

1520 → Battle of Raichur → Krishnadevaraya Victory

45. Opponent at Raichur

  • The Bijapur Sultan at the time was Ismail Adil Shah.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raichur 1520 → Krishnadevaraya vs Ismail Adil Shah

46. Importance of Raichur Victory

  • It significantly increased Krishnadevaraya's prestige.
  • Contemporary Portuguese accounts describe the enormous Vijayanagara army and celebrations.

47. Gajapati Kingdom

  • The Gajapati rulers controlled Odisha and important parts of coastal Andhra.
  • They were major eastern rivals of Vijayanagara.

48. Prataparudra Deva

  • Gajapati ruler Prataparudra Deva fought Krishnadevaraya.
  • Vijayanagara campaigns pushed northward into Andhra-Odisha frontier regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Krishnadevaraya → Gajapati Prataparudra

49. Udayagiri Campaign

  • Udayagiri was an important fort captured by Krishnadevaraya during campaigns against the Gajapatis.

50. Kondavidu

  • Kondavidu was another important Andhra fort brought under Vijayanagara authority.

51. Vijayanagara–Gajapati Settlement

  • Conflict was followed by a political settlement.
  • Matrimonial traditions are associated with the peace, though details differ in sources.

52. Krishnadevaraya and Portuguese

  • Krishnadevaraya maintained diplomatic and commercial relations with the Portuguese.
  • Portuguese coastal power facilitated access to imported horses and firearms.

53. Portuguese Capture of Goa

  • The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 under Afonso de Albuquerque.
  • Goa became a major Portuguese commercial base on India's west coast.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Goa → Portuguese → 1510 → Albuquerque

54. Vijayanagara–Portuguese Trade

Vijayanagara obtained:

  • Horses.
  • Metals.
  • Military goods.

The Portuguese obtained:

  • Textiles.
  • Rice.
  • Spices.
  • Other Indian commodities.

55. Domingo Paes

  • Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited Vijayanagara during Krishnadevaraya's reign.
  • His account gives valuable information about:
  • City life.
  • Festivals.
  • Military organisation.
  • Markets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Domingo Paes → Krishnadevaraya

56. Paes on Vijayanagara

He described:

  • A vast city.
  • Rich markets.
  • Large population.
  • Elaborate royal ceremonies.
  • Strong military forces.

57. Mahanavami Festival

  • The Mahanavami or Dasara celebrations were major royal ceremonies.
  • The king reviewed:
  • Troops.
  • Horses.
  • Elephants.
  • Nobles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahanavami → Royal Festival of Vijayanagara

58. Mahanavami Dibba

  • Mahanavami Dibba is a massive ceremonial platform in the royal centre at Hampi.
  • It was associated with imperial festivals and displays.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahanavami Dibba → Hampi

59. Fernao Nuniz

  • Portuguese chronicler Fernao Nuniz visited Vijayanagara during the sixteenth century, around the period following Krishnadevaraya.
  • He recorded traditions about:
  • Vijayanagara's foundation.
  • Battles.
  • Court politics.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fernao Nuniz → Vijayanagara Chronicle

60. Duarte Barbosa

  • Duarte Barbosa wrote about Indian Ocean trade and South India in the early sixteenth century.
  • His account provides information on:
  • Ports.
  • Trade.
  • Social groups.

61. Krishnadevaraya — Scholar-King

  • Krishnadevaraya was both:
  • Military ruler.
  • Literary patron.
  • He wrote works in Telugu and Sanskrit.

62. Amuktamalyada

  • Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu.
  • It is his most famous literary work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amuktamalyada → Krishnadevaraya → Telugu

63. Theme of Amuktamalyada

  • The work centres on Andal and Vishnu devotion.
  • It also contains observations on kingship and administration.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Cultural Link

Amuktamalyada → Andal Tradition

64. Andal

  • Andal is one of the twelve Alvars of the Tamil Vaishnava tradition.
  • Her association gives Amuktamalyada a significant Tamil cultural connection.

65. Jambavati Kalyanam

  • Krishnadevaraya is also associated with the Sanskrit work Jambavati Kalyanam.

66. Andhra Bhoja

  • Krishnadevaraya is traditionally called Andhra Bhoja because of his patronage of Telugu literature.
📌 Must-Memorise

Andhra Bhoja → Krishnadevaraya

67. Ashtadiggajas

  • Tradition refers to eight eminent Telugu poets at Krishnadevaraya's court as the Ashtadiggajas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ashtadiggajas → Eight Telugu Poets → Krishnadevaraya

68. Allasani Peddana

  • Allasani Peddana was one of the greatest poets of Krishnadevaraya's court.
  • He is traditionally called Andhra Kavita Pitamaha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Andhra Kavita Pitamaha → Allasani Peddana

69. Manucharitramu

  • Allasani Peddana wrote Manucharitramu, also known as Swarochisha Manu Sambhavam.

70. Nandi Timmana

  • Nandi Timmana was one of the Ashtadiggajas.
  • He is associated with Parijataapaharanamu.

71. Dhurjati

  • Dhurjati was an important Telugu poet associated with the Srikalahasti tradition.

72. Tenali Ramakrishna

  • Tenali Ramakrishna was a Telugu poet traditionally associated with Krishnadevaraya's court.
  • He later became famous in popular folklore for wit and intelligence.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Tenali Rama Stories → Many Are Later Folklore

73. Pingali Surana

  • Pingali Surana was an important Telugu literary figure of the Vijayanagara cultural world.
  • He is commonly included in the traditional Ashtadiggaja list.

74. Literature Under Vijayanagara

The empire patronised:

  • Telugu.
  • Kannada.
  • Sanskrit.
  • Tamil.

75. Telugu Literature

  • Telugu literature flourished greatly under the Tuluva rulers.
  • Krishnadevaraya's reign is particularly celebrated.

76. Kannada Literature

Important Kannada religious and literary traditions continued under:

  • Virashaiva writers.
  • Haridasa saints.
  • Court poets.

77. Sanskrit Scholarship

  • Sanskrit remained important in:
  • Theology.
  • Philosophy.
  • Court scholarship.
  • Religious institutions.

78. Tamil Literature

  • Tamil literary activity continued under Vijayanagara and the later Nayak polities.
  • Temple-centred religious literature and commentarial traditions remained important.

79. Vyasatirtha

  • Vyasatirtha was an important Dvaita Vedanta scholar associated with Vijayanagara.
  • He enjoyed royal patronage, especially during Krishnadevaraya's period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vyasatirtha → Dvaita → Krishnadevaraya Period

80. Purandaradasa

  • Purandaradasa was a major Haridasa saint-composer.
  • He is traditionally called the "Father of Carnatic Music."
📌 Must-Memorise

Purandaradasa → Father of Carnatic Music

81. Kanakadasa

  • Kanakadasa was another important Haridasa saint-poet.
  • He composed devotional works in Kannada.

82. Haridasa Movement

  • The Haridasa tradition promoted Vaishnava bhakti through:
  • Music.
  • Poetry.
  • Vernacular devotional compositions.

83. Krishnadevaraya and Temples

He patronised major temples across South India.

Important associations include:

  • Tirupati.
  • Hampi.
  • Kanchipuram and other major temple centres through imperial patronage.

84. Tirupati

  • Krishnadevaraya made important donations to the Tirumala-Tirupati temple.
  • Inscriptions record his visits and gifts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Krishnadevaraya → Tirupati Patronage

85. Krishnadevaraya's Death

  • Krishnadevaraya died in 1529.
  • His death was followed by increasing political instability.

86. Achyuta Devaraya

  • Achyuta Devaraya succeeded Krishnadevaraya.
  • He ruled during a period of increasing factional competition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Krishnadevaraya → Achyuta Devaraya

87. Achyutaraya Temple

  • The Achyutaraya Temple at Hampi is associated with Achyuta Devaraya's period.

88. Sadasiva Raya

  • Sadasiva Raya later became nominal emperor.
  • Real political power was increasingly exercised by Aliya Rama Raya.

89. Aliya Rama Raya

  • Rama Raya was a powerful Vijayanagara statesman and military leader.
  • He was the son-in-law of Krishnadevaraya.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aliya Rama Raya → Son-in-Law of Krishnadevaraya

90. Meaning of Aliya

  • In Kannada, Aliya means son-in-law.
  • Hence the title Aliya Rama Raya.

91. Rama Raya's Deccan Policy

  • Rama Raya intervened repeatedly in disputes among the Deccan Sultanates.
  • Vijayanagara alternately allied with one Sultanate against another.

92. Deccan Sultanates

After the breakup of the Bahmani Sultanate, major successor states included:

  • Ahmadnagar.
  • Bijapur.
  • Golconda.
  • Bidar.
  • Berar.

93. Political Consequence of Rama Raya's Policy

  • Repeated Vijayanagara intervention eventually encouraged several Deccan Sultanates to unite against Rama Raya.

94. Battle of Talikota

  • The Battle of Talikota was fought in 1565.
  • Vijayanagara forces were defeated by an alliance of Deccan Sultanates.
📌 Must-Memorise

1565 → Battle of Talikota

95. Other Names of Talikota Battle

The battle is also called:

  • Battle of Rakshasa-Tangadi.
  • Battle of Bannihatti in some accounts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Talikota = Rakshasa-Tangadi

96. Vijayanagara Leader at Talikota

  • Rama Raya was the dominant Vijayanagara commander.
  • He was captured and killed during the battle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Talikota → Rama Raya Killed

97. Sultanates at Talikota

The principal anti-Vijayanagara alliance included rulers of:

  • Bijapur.
  • Ahmadnagar.
  • Golconda.
  • Bidar.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Berar → Usually Not Listed as a Principal Participant in Talikota Alliance

98. Result of Talikota

  • The Vijayanagara army was decisively defeated.
  • The capital was subsequently occupied and extensively plundered.

99. Talikota Did Not Immediately End the Empire

  • The empire survived after 1565.
  • The capital shifted away from Hampi.
  • The Aravidu dynasty continued Vijayanagara rule.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

1565 Talikota ≠ Immediate End of Vijayanagara Dynasty

100. Aravidu Dynasty

  • The Aravidu dynasty became the final ruling dynasty of Vijayanagara.
  • Tirumala Deva Raya founded the new ruling line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Final Vijayanagara Dynasty → Aravidu

101. Tirumala Deva Raya

  • Tirumala was Rama Raya's brother.
  • After Talikota he transferred the imperial centre away from devastated Vijayanagara.

102. Penukonda

  • Penukonda became an important capital of the Aravidu rulers after Hampi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Post-Talikota Capital → Penukonda

103. Chandragiri

  • Chandragiri later became another important Vijayanagara capital.
  • It is located in present-day Andhra Pradesh near Tirupati.
📌 Must-Memorise

Later Vijayanagara Capital → Chandragiri

104. Vellore

  • Vellore also became an important late Vijayanagara political centre.
  • This strengthened the empire's connection with northern Tamil Nadu.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Late Vijayanagara Centre → Vellore

105. Chandragiri and Chennai History

  • The later Vijayanagara rulers at Chandragiri controlled territories extending toward the Coromandel Coast.
  • Local Nayaks under this political framework played a role in early seventeenth-century coastal grants.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Late Vijayanagara → Chandragiri → Coromandel Political Context

106. Decline of Aravidu Authority

The final phase was weakened by:

  • Deccan Sultanate pressure.
  • Powerful Nayaks.
  • Succession disputes.
  • Loss of revenue.
  • Fragmentation.

107. Nayankara System

  • Vijayanagara administration relied heavily on military chiefs called Nayakas.
  • The system is often called:
  • Nayankara system.
  • Amaranayaka system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vijayanagara → Nayankara / Amaranayaka System

108. Amaranayaka

  • Amaranayakas received territorial revenue assignments called amaram.
  • In return they:
  • Maintained troops.
  • Paid tribute.
  • Supported the emperor militarily.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amaram → Revenue Assignment to Nayaka

109. Nayakas

Nayakas were expected to maintain:

  • Infantry.
  • Cavalry.
  • Elephants where required.
  • Forts.

110. Nayaka Authority

  • Nayakas exercised substantial regional authority.
  • Strong emperors could control them.
  • Under weak rulers, many Nayakas became increasingly autonomous.

111. Nayaka System and Fragmentation

  • The growth of powerful Nayaka houses contributed to political decentralisation after the sixteenth century.

112. Nayaks of Tamil Nadu

Important Vijayanagara-derived Nayak states included:

  • Madurai.
  • Thanjavur.
  • Gingee.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nayak States → Madurai + Thanjavur + Gingee

113. Madurai Nayaks

  • Madurai Nayaks developed from Vijayanagara provincial administration.
  • They later became effectively independent.

114. Viswanatha Nayak

  • Viswanatha Nayak is traditionally regarded as the founder of the Madurai Nayak dynasty.
  • He ruled during the sixteenth century.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Madurai Nayak Founder → Viswanatha Nayak

115. Ariyanatha Mudaliar

  • Ariyanatha Mudaliar was an important minister and military commander under the Madurai Nayaks.
  • He is traditionally associated with organisation of the Palayakkarar system.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Ariyanatha Mudaliar → Palayakkarar System

116. Palayakkarar

  • Palayakkarars or Poligars controlled military-revenue units called palayams.
  • They became important in later Tamil political history.
📌 Must-Memorise

Palayam → Palayakkarar / Polygar

117. Thanjavur Nayaks

  • Thanjavur also emerged as an important Nayak state under Vijayanagara influence.
  • It became a major centre of:
  • Temple patronage.
  • Literature.
  • Music.

118. Gingee Nayaks

  • Gingee became another important Vijayanagara-derived Nayak centre in northern Tamil Nadu.

119. Central Administration

  • Vijayanagara was a monarchy.
  • The emperor was the supreme:
  • Military authority.
  • Administrative authority.
  • Judicial authority.

120. Royal Succession

  • Kingship was hereditary in principle.
  • Actual succession often involved:
  • Brothers.
  • Sons.
  • Regents.
  • Military factions.

121. Royal Council

The emperor was assisted by:

  • Ministers.
  • Military commanders.
  • Provincial governors.
  • Court officials.

122. Mahapradhani

  • Mahapradhani was an important high-ranking minister.
  • The term broadly corresponds to a chief minister in several contexts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mahapradhani → High Minister

123. Dandanayaka

  • Dandanayaka was a title used for important military or administrative officials.

124. Administrative Divisions

The terminology varied across regions, but divisions could include:

  • Rajya or Mandala.
  • Nadu.
  • Sthala.
  • Grama.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Vijayanagara Administrative Terms → Varied Across Regions and Periods

125. Rajya / Mandala

  • Large provincial territories were often described as Rajyas or Mandalas.

126. Nadu

  • Nadu represented an important intermediate territorial unit with older South Indian roots.

127. Grama

  • Grama or village formed the basic rural settlement and revenue unit.

128. Ayagar System

  • Village administration in many Vijayanagara territories involved hereditary officials collectively known as Ayagars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ayagar System → Village Administration

129. Ayagars

Ayagars performed functions relating to:

  • Revenue.
  • Records.
  • Security.
  • Irrigation.
  • Village services.

130. Hereditary Village Offices

  • Many village offices became hereditary.
  • Officials were compensated through:
  • Land assignments.
  • Shares of produce.
  • Fees.

131. Village Autonomy

  • Local institutions continued to perform important functions.
  • However, royal and Nayaka authorities increasingly influenced village revenue administration.

132. Revenue

Major sources included:

  • Land revenue.
  • Customs.
  • Professional taxes.
  • Market taxes.
  • Tribute from Nayakas.
  • Trade duties.

133. Land Revenue

  • Agriculture was the principal source of state income.
  • Revenue varied by:
  • Crop.
  • Soil.
  • Irrigation.
  • Local conditions.

134. Irrigated Land

  • Irrigated land generally had higher productivity and higher revenue value than dry land.

135. Taxes

Historical records mention taxes on:

  • Agriculture.
  • Houses.
  • Markets.
  • Crafts.
  • Marriage in some contexts.
  • Livestock and professional activities.
